questions.q: In the common four-tier commercial classification scheme described in this lesson, which tier is described as fine for anyone, inside or outside the organization, to see?
options: Public
Internal
Confidential
Restricted
questions.explain: Public covers information like marketing material or published pricing — there's no harm in anyone seeing it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what actually makes a classification tier meaningful, beyond its name?
options: The color used to display the label in software
The alphabetical order of the tier names
Defined answers to who can access it, what happens if it leaks, and what controls apply
Whether the tier name sounds more serious than another tier's name
questions.explain: The lesson frames the tier name as shorthand for a pre-agreed answer to three questions: access, consequence of a leak, and required controls.

questions.q: Why is it acceptable that different organizations use 3, 4, or 5 tiers with different label names?
options: It isn't acceptable — every organization must use exactly four tiers named Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted
What matters is a small number of clearly defined tiers consistently applied, not the exact names or count
Because classification schemes have no real effect on how data is handled
Because tier names are standardized by international law
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly says the transferable skill is recognizing the pattern — a small, consistent, clearly defined set of tiers — not memorizing one specific label set.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the relationship between the US government's Confidential/Secret/Top Secret system and commercial data classification?
options: They are the same scheme, just with different names for the same tiers
The government scheme is a stricter version that all companies should adopt
They are genuinely different schemes — the government one is legally defined for national security information and should not be conflated with commercial classification
The government scheme replaced commercial data classification entirely
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that conflating the two is a category error — the government/military scheme is a legally-defined, separately administered system for a different purpose.

questions.q: What is the 'transferable skill' this lesson says is worth building, regarding classification schemes?
options: Memorizing the exact label names used by one specific vendor
Recognizing the general pattern — a small number of tiers, each with defined access, consequence, and control answers — so you can map it onto whatever scheme an employer uses
Learning to design a classification scheme with as many tiers as possible
Reciting the government's Top Secret clearance process from memory
questions.explain: The lesson closes by saying you'll find some tiered scheme at every job, under different names — the useful skill is recognizing the underlying pattern quickly, not memorizing one organization's exact labels.
